summary: An older allergy medicine (antihistamine) that also blocks serotonin. It is used for allergies, to boost appetite in children, to prevent migraines and cyclic vomiting, and as an add-on in serotonin syndrome, but it often causes sleepiness, weight gain and drying side effects.
description: Cyproheptadine (Periactin) is an older (first-generation) antihistamine that also blocks serotonin. It was introduced in 1961. In psychiatry and children's medicine it is used less for allergy and more for other (off-label) uses: boosting appetite in long-term illness, preventing migraines in children, cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS), long-lasting stomach pain without a clear cause (functional abdominal pain), and as an add-on in moderate serotonin syndrome. Sleepiness, weight gain and strong drying side effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, trouble peeing, confusion in older adults) are expected. Liver damage and blood problems are rare but have been reported. Because of this, it is generally avoided in older adults and used carefully in people who already take other drying medicines or who have heart, weight or blood-sugar risks, or liver disease.
patient_summary:
Cyproheptadine (Periactin) is an older allergy medicine that also blocks serotonin. Doctors sometimes use it to help kids eat more and gain weight, to prevent migraines or cyclic vomiting, or as an add-on in certain cases of serotonin syndrome.

It commonly causes sleepiness, increased appetite, and weight gain. It can also cause dry mouth, constipation, and sometimes confusion—especially in older adults, so it is usually avoided in people over 65. Rarely, it has been linked to liver problems or blood count changes.

Dosing is weight-based in children and is usually given 2–4 times per day. Your prescriber will check for sleepiness, weight gain, and any signs of liver or blood problems if you are on it long term.

primary.condition_name: Allergic rhinitis and urticaria (though second-generation antihistamines preferred)
Pediatric appetite stimulation in chronic disease (off-label)

secondary.context: Year-round and seasonal hay fever, non-allergic runny nose (vasomotor rhinitis) and allergic eye irritation; not usually tried first because of sleepiness and drying side effects.
Mild, uncomplicated hives and swelling under the skin (angioedema); newer antihistamines are preferred.
Spasticity associated with spinal cord damage; evidence mixed and overall limited.

off_label.context: Appetite stimulation and weight gain in pediatric oncology and other chronic disease populations; ~70–80% response in small trials.
Added on to boost appetite in malnourished or underweight children when non-medicine approaches have not helped enough.
Pediatric migraine prevention; often considered in younger children where sedation and weight gain may be more tolerable.
Usually tried first for prevention in children under 5 with frequent or severe cyclic vomiting episodes; less favored in older children because of weight gain and sleepiness.
Long-lasting stomach pain or indigestion that has not improved with standard treatment; small studies show it helps only some people.
Added on for moderate serotonin syndrome when agitation continues despite benzodiazepines and supportive care, because it blocks serotonin.

therapeutic_response.display: Sleepiness and drying effects (such as dry mouth) usually start within a few hours of a dose; increased appetite and weight gain come on over days to weeks.

common_adverse_effects.notes: When it is used for appetite or migraine prevention, more of the dose is often given at bedtime. Daytime doses may be limited by sleepiness, especially when starting or raising the dose.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation and other drying effects
common_adverse_effects.notes: Dry mouth, constipation, trouble peeing and blurry vision get worse at higher doses and add up with other drying medicines. If you are at high risk of constipation, your prescriber may suggest a plan to prevent it.
Desirable in underweight or FTT populations, but problematic in patients near or above ideal weight, especially if used long-term.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness, or feeling faint when standing up
common_adverse_effects.notes: Counsel on slow positional changes, especially in patients on antihypertensives or with baseline autonomic dysfunction.
Young children may exhibit paradoxical excitation, irritability, or insomnia rather than sedation.

serious_risks.risk: Hepatic failure and hepatitis: Rare but potentially fatal; consider baseline and follow-up LFTs with prolonged or high-dose use.

Blood problems: a dangerous drop in white blood cells (infection risk), low platelets (bleeding risk) and breakdown of red blood cells (hemolytic anemia); a blood count is checked if these are suspected.
Seizures: Reported in overdose and with excessive dosing, especially in infants and young children.
Severe poisoning from its drying effects: sudden confusion (delirium), overheating, being unable to pee, and a stopped bowel; the risk is higher in overdose or with several drying medicines.
Low blood pressure and fast heart rhythms: rare but important in people with heart disease.
Anaphylaxis and severe hypersensitivity reactions: Require immediate discontinuation and emergency care.

safety.black_box_warning: No FDA boxed warning. The main concerns are sleepiness, poisoning from its drying effects (especially in older adults), and rare liver damage and blood problems.

contraindications.contraindication: Allergy to this medicine or any of its ingredients
Older or frail people (per labeling and Beers Criteria)
Known severe liver failure (usually avoided, given reports of liver damage)

precautions: Sleepiness and slower reactions: avoid it if your job needs you to stay alert for safety (e.g., pilots, commercial drivers, heavy machinery operators). Be careful driving or using equipment until you know how it affects you.

Drying effects: these add up with tricyclic antidepressants, clozapine, older low-potency antipsychotics, bladder medicines and others, raising the risk of constipation, trouble peeing, blurred vision, fast heartbeat and sudden confusion (delirium).

Liver damage: rare cases of liver inflammation (hepatitis) and liver failure have been reported. Liver blood tests before and during treatment may be considered with long-term or high-dose use, especially if you already have liver disease.

Blood problems: reports after approval include a dangerous drop in white blood cells, breakdown of red blood cells, and low platelets. Unexplained infection, bleeding or bruising should be checked with a blood count.

Heart effects: low blood pressure, fast heartbeat and palpitations have been reported. Use caution with structural heart disease, heart-rhythm problems, or other medicines that affect the QT (though this medicine itself is not a major QT risk).
Paradoxical CNS excitation: Especially in younger children—may present as irritability, insomnia, or behavioral disinhibition.
Overdose risk: as with other older antihistamines, an overdose can cause severe drying-effect poisoning, seizures and heart-rhythm problems.

interactions.mechanism: Should not be used together. Taking them together may strengthen drying effects and effects on the brain; the label says not to combine them.
interactions.action: Avoid co-prescribing. Allow adequate washout when switching in either direction.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS Depressants (benzodiazepines, sedating antipsychotics, opioids, alcohol)
interactions.mechanism: More sleepiness, slower reactions and coordination, and a higher risk of falls and accidents.
interactions.action: Use lowest effective doses; counsel patients on avoiding alcohol and high-risk activities; avoid in older adults when possible.

interactions.interactant: Psychiatric and other medicines with strong drying effects (TCAs, clozapine, low-potency FGAs, paroxetine, oxybutynin, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Drying effects add up: constipation, trouble peeing, memory and thinking problems, sudden confusion (delirium), fast heartbeat.
interactions.action: Review how many drying medicines you take in total and choose ones without this effect where possible. Watch bowel habits, thinking and peeing.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that raise serotonin (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans, etc.) in serotonin syndrome
interactions.mechanism: This medicine is used as an antidote that blocks serotonin in serotonin syndrome, but it should not be used to hide ongoing serotonin poisoning while the medicines causing it are continued.
interactions.action: In serotonin syndrome, all medicines raising serotonin must be stopped; this medicine is used only as an add-on with benzodiazepines and supportive care in moderate cases.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that can harm the liver (valproate, isoniazid, certain antipsychotics, etc.)
interactions.mechanism: Possible added risk to the liver, as this medicine has rare but documented cases of liver damage.
interactions.action: Liver blood tests before and during treatment may be considered when combining several medicines that can harm the liver; report any signs of liver trouble early.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Sleepiness and thinking: daytime sleepiness, attention, and reaction speed — especially in school-aged children and people in safety-sensitive jobs
Weight/BMI and metabolic profile: At baseline and regularly in appetite-stimulation, migraine, and CVS uses; intervene early if excessive weight gain occurs.
Bowel and bladder: constipation, trouble starting to pee, or being unable to pee, at each visit, especially if you take other drying medicines
Liver blood tests: may be checked before and during long-term or higher-dose treatment, or if you have liver disease or take other medicines that can harm the liver
CBC: Not required routinely, but obtain if clinical signs suggest cytopenias (recurrent infections, bruising, fatigue).
Behavior and sleep in children: Monitor for paradoxical excitation, irritability, insomnia, or behavioral disinhibition.
Medicine review: regularly going over all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal products to see how many cause sleepiness or drying effects

special_populations.pregnancy: Limited human data do not show a clear risk of harm to a developing baby, but the numbers are small, and older antihistamines are generally not preferred because of sleepiness and drying effects. If an antihistamine by mouth is needed in pregnancy, other medicines with better safety records are usually chosen.
special_populations.lactation: It is not known whether it passes into breast milk. Based on experience with similar medicines (sleepy or irritable babies, possible effects on prolactin and milk supply) and the product label, it should not be used while breastfeeding.
special_populations.pediatric: Widely used off-label in children ≥2 years for appetite stimulation, migraine, CVS, and functional abdominal pain. Requires careful attention to dosing, sedation, behavior change (including paradoxical excitation), and weight/BMI tracking.
special_populations.geriatric: Avoid in people 65 and older (Beers Criteria), because its strong drying and sedating effects raise the risk of confusion, falls, constipation and being unable to pee.
special_populations.renal_impairment: The body clears it more slowly when the kidneys are not working well; it is started at a lower dose and raised slowly, watching for stronger or longer-lasting effects.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Use with caution; the liver breaks it down, and rare cases of liver inflammation (hepatitis) and liver failure have been described. Liver blood tests before starting and from time to time may be considered if long-term use is planned.

pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Not precisely quantified, but oral absorption is considered good.
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Metabolites ~16 hours; clinical sedative effect shorter and dose-dependent.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Primarily hepatic via glucuronidation to inactive metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (~40%, primarily as metabolites), feces (2–20%; <6% as unchanged drug).
pharmacokinetics.protein_binding: Not fully characterized; clinically behaves as moderately protein-bound.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: No clinically significant food effect described.

dosing.titration: Dosing is generally weight-based in children and fixed in adults. Start low and titrate based on indication, efficacy, and tolerability, with particular attention to sedation and anticholinergic effects.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Cyproheptadine does not cause physiologic dependence. However, abrupt discontinuation can be associated with recurrence of target symptoms (eg, appetite loss, migraine, CVS) and, rarely, rebound allergic symptoms.

sections.heading: Key Clinical Uses
sections.text: Cyproheptadine has largely been replaced by second-generation antihistamines for routine allergy care, but remains a useful tool in specific pediatric and consultation-liaison psychiatry scenarios due to its antiserotonergic and appetite-stimulating properties.
items: {link:condition:allergic-rhinitis:Allergic conditions}: Seasonal/perennial allergic rhinitis, vasomotor rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, urticaria, angioedema, adjunctive therapy in anaphylaxis. Typically not first-line; reserve for patients who tolerate sedation and anticholinergic effects.

{link:condition:cancer-related-anorexia:Appetite stimulation}: Off-label use for decreased appetite and weight loss in chronic illness (eg, pediatric oncology, cystic fibrosis, neurodevelopmental disorders) when non-pharmacologic strategies and nutritional support are insufficient.
{link:condition:migraine:Childhood migraine prophylaxis}: Low-cost option for younger patients, particularly when weight gain and sedation may be acceptable or even beneficial.

{link:condition:cyclic-vomiting-syndrome:Cyclic vomiting syndrome prophylaxis}: First-line prophylaxis in children <5 years; effect size in older youth more modest and limited by weight gain/sedation.
{link:condition:functional-abdominal-pain:Functional abdominal pain / dyspeptic syndrome}: For refractory cases in which standard GI and behavioral interventions have failed.

{link:condition:serotonin-syndrome:Serotonin syndrome (moderate)}: Adjunctive antiserotonergic agent when agitation persists despite discontinuation of serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, and supportive care.
off_label: Spasticity associated with spinal cord damage (weak evidence)
Adjunct in multifactorial pediatric feeding disorders (eg, cleft palate, neurodevelopmental disability)
Non-specific ‘sedating antihistamine’ use for insomnia (discouraged due to anticholinergic burden)

sections.heading: Typical Clinical Course & Patient-Reported Effects

quotes: Parents often report that the child is ‘sleepier’ or ‘calmer’ during the day, especially after dose escalations.
Adults may endorse grogginess, slowed thinking, and decreased vigilance, particularly in the first days of therapy or with higher doses.
items.note: Sedation is dose- and timing-dependent and can be partially managed by bedtime-weighted dosing.

quotes: Families frequently describe a noticeable increase in interest in food within days to weeks.
Weight gain can be clinically meaningful in underweight patients, but can quickly become excessive in those near normal weight.
items.note: Regular weight/BMI monitoring is essential; appetite effects may wane over time in some patients.

quotes: Dry mouth, constipation, and blurry vision are common with dose escalation.
In younger children, paradoxical excitation or irritability may occur instead of sedation.
items.note: Watch cumulative anticholinergic burden when combined with TCAs, antipsychotics, bladder antimuscarinics, etc.

quotes: Younger children often tolerate sedation and weight gain better than adolescents and adults.
Older adults frequently experience confusion and orthostatic symptoms—use is generally avoided.
items.note: Beers Criteria list cyproheptadine as ‘avoid’ in adults ≥65 due to strong anticholinergic effects.

sections.intro: From a psychiatrist’s perspective, these are common patterns you’re likely to see in practice:

sections.heading: Onset & Duration in Practice
sections.text: Cyproheptadine’s sedating and appetite-stimulating effects generally precede any disease-specific benefit.
key_points: Sedation: Onset within hours of initial dosing; often maximal in the first few days, then partially attenuates.
Appetite stimulation: Typically emerges within 3–7 days, with measurable weight changes over weeks.
Migraine/CVS prophylaxis: Evaluate efficacy over several weeks; dose adjustments guided by response and tolerability.
Serotonin syndrome add-on: when used, a loading dose (e.g., 12 mg) followed by 2 mg every 2 hours can work within hours in people who respond.
Elimination: Metabolite half-life ~16 hours; dosing 2–4 times daily is standard due to clinical effect profile.

sections.heading: Evidence Snapshot
sections.text: In pediatric oncology and chronic disease populations, cyproheptadine (≈0.25 mg/kg/day divided BID–QID) has been associated with clinically meaningful weight gain or stabilization in the majority of patients. Similar benefits have been observed in malnourished children and those with multifactorial feeding problems.
sections.metric: Response rate in pediatric appetite stimulation
sections.comparison: Placebo-controlled data are limited; most data from open-label or small randomized studies.
sections.clinical_details: Open-label and small randomized controlled trials report ~70–80% of children experiencing either weight gain or prevention of further loss, with mean weight gains around 2–3 kg over 8–12 weeks. Subgroup analyses suggest greater responsiveness in older children (>9 years) and those with hematologic malignancies. In cystic fibrosis, 12-week trials using 12 mg/day showed significantly greater weight gain versus placebo. Data for migraine and CVS prophylaxis are less robust but support a trial in appropriate patients.

citation.authors: Multiple authors (pediatric oncology, CF, malnutrition cohorts)
citation.title: Cyproheptadine for appetite stimulation and weight gain in children with chronic disease

sections.heading: Critical Safety & Prescribing Considerations
sections.highlight: Cyproheptadine is a strongly anticholinergic, sedating first-generation antihistamine. In psychiatry it should be used tactically, with explicit attention to delirium, falls, hepatic function, and metabolic effects.
sections.black_box: No FDA boxed warning. Major concerns include sedation, anticholinergic toxicity (especially in older adults), rare hepatotoxicity, and hematologic toxicity.
other: Sedation and impaired psychomotor performance: avoid in people with safety-sensitive jobs (e.g., pilots, commercial drivers, heavy machinery operators). Counsel about driving and operating equipment.
Anticholinergic burden: Additive with TCAs, clozapine, low-potency FGAs, bladder antimuscarinics, etc. Increases risk of constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, and delirium.
Hepatotoxicity: rare cases of hepatitis and hepatic failure have been reported. Consider baseline and periodic LFTs with chronic or high-dose use, particularly in people with existing liver disease.
Hematologic toxicity: Postmarketing reports of agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Unexplained infection, bleeding, or bruising warrants CBC evaluation.

Cardiovascular effects: Hypotension, tachycardia, and palpitations reported; use caution in structural heart disease, arrhythmias, and those on QT-active regimens (though cyproheptadine itself is not a major QT prolonger).
Paradoxical CNS excitation: Especially in younger children—may present as irritability, insomnia, or behavioral disinhibition.
Overdose risk: As with other first-generation antihistamines, overdose can cause severe anticholinergic toxicity, seizures, and arrhythmias.
patient_counseling: Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or engaging in high-risk activities until individual sedative effects are known.
Monitor for constipation, urinary retention, or blurry vision; report these promptly.
Report right-upper-quadrant pain, dark urine, jaundice, or unexplained fatigue—these could indicate liver problems.
Keep out of reach of children—accidental overdose in young children can be life-threatening.
Do not combine with other over-the-counter ‘PM’ products, antihistamines, or sedatives without checking with the prescriber.

sections.heading: Adverse Effects
sections.summary: Cyproheptadine shares the class effects of first-generation antihistamines—sedation, anticholinergic symptoms, and weight gain—plus rare but serious hepatic and hematologic events.
plain_language_list: Dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy or retention
Rare: Liver injury, low blood counts, seizures, severe allergic reactions

common.patient_note: Plan bedtime-weighted dosing when using for appetite or migraine prophylaxis. Daytime dosing may be limited by somnolence, especially during initiation and dose escalations.
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, and blurry vision are dose-related and cumulative with other anticholinergics. Consider prophylactic bowel regimen in high-risk patients.
Desirable in underweight or FTT populations, but problematic in patients near or above ideal weight, especially if used long-term.
Counsel on slow positional changes, especially in patients on antihypertensives or with baseline autonomic dysfunction.
Young children may exhibit paradoxical excitation, irritability, or insomnia rather than sedation.

serious: Hepatic failure and hepatitis: Rare but potentially fatal; consider baseline and follow-up LFTs with prolonged or high-dose use.
Hematologic toxicity: Agranulocytosis, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia; monitor CBC if clinical suspicion arises.
Seizures: Reported in overdose and with excessive dosing, especially in infants and young children.
Severe anticholinergic toxicity: Delirium, hyperthermia, urinary retention, ileus; risk amplified in overdose or with multiple anticholinergics.
Hypotension and tachyarrhythmias: Rare but clinically relevant in those with underlying cardiovascular disease.
Anaphylaxis and severe hypersensitivity reactions: Require immediate discontinuation and emergency care.

sections.heading: Key Drug Interactions (Psychiatry-Relevant)

items.risk: Contraindicated. Combined use may potentiate anticholinergic and CNS effects; labeling prohibits concurrent use.
items.action: Avoid co-prescribing. Allow adequate washout when switching in either direction.

items.with: Other CNS Depressants (benzodiazepines, sedating antipsychotics, opioids, alcohol)
items.risk: Additive sedation, impaired psychomotor function, increased fall and accident risk.
items.action: Use lowest effective doses; counsel patients on avoiding alcohol and high-risk activities; avoid in older adults when possible.

items.with: Strong Anticholinergic Psychotropics (TCAs, clozapine, low-potency FGAs, paroxetine, oxybutynin, etc.)
items.risk: Cumulative anticholinergic burden: constipation, urinary retention, cognitive impairment, delirium, tachycardia.
items.action: Assess total anticholinergic load. Prefer non-anticholinergic alternatives if possible. Monitor bowel function, cognition, and urinary status.

items.with: Serotonergic Agents (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans, etc.) in Serotonin Syndrome
items.risk: Cyproheptadine is used as an antiserotonergic antidote in serotonin syndrome, but should not be used to ‘mask’ ongoing serotonergic toxicity while serotonergic agents are continued.
items.action: Ensure all offending serotonergic agents are discontinued in serotonin syndrome; use cyproheptadine only as adjunct with benzodiazepines and supportive care in moderate cases.

items.with: Hepatotoxic Drugs (valproate, isoniazid, certain antipsychotics, etc.)
items.risk: Potential additive hepatic risk given rare but documented cyproheptadine hepatotoxicity.
items.action: Consider baseline and periodic LFTs when combining multiple hepatotoxic agents; maintain low threshold for evaluation of hepatic symptoms.

sections.intro: Cyproheptadine has fewer high-risk pharmacokinetic interactions than many psychotropics, but adds substantially to sedative and anticholinergic load and is contraindicated with MAOIs.

sections.heading: Discontinuation & Tapering
sections.text: Cyproheptadine does not cause physiologic dependence. However, abrupt discontinuation can be associated with recurrence of target symptoms (eg, appetite loss, migraine, CVS) and, rarely, rebound allergic symptoms.
key_points: No formal taper is required from a withdrawal standpoint.
In practice, gradual dose reductions (eg, 25–50% every 1–2 weeks) can help distinguish relapse from transient discontinuation effects.
For appetite stimulation, taper after weight stabilization or after a defined trial period (eg, 8–12 weeks) to determine ongoing need.
In migraine/CVS prophylaxis, maintain therapy for a defined period of stability (eg, several months) before considering a slow taper.
In serotonin syndrome, cyproheptadine is short-term and should be discontinued once serotonin toxicity has clearly resolved.

sections.heading: Dosing Overview
sections.text: Dosing is generally weight-based in children and fixed in adults. Start low and titrate based on indication, efficacy, and tolerability, with particular attention to sedation and anticholinergic effects.

adult.allergic_maintenance: 4–20 mg/day in divided doses; some people may need up to 32 mg/day.
adult.appetite_off_label: 2 mg PO QID for 1 week, then increase to 4 mg PO QID as tolerated (monitor sedation and weight).
adult.serotonin_syndrome_off_label: 12 mg PO once, then 2 mg PO q2h until clinical response; maintenance 4–8 mg q6h PRN; maximum 32 mg/day.
adult.older_adults: Avoid use (Beers Criteria) due to strong anticholinergic effects and delirium/fall risk.
adult.renal_impairment: No formal adjustment; elimination is reduced in renal insufficiency—start at lower end of dose range and titrate cautiously.
adult.hepatic_impairment: No formal dose guidance, but given hepatic metabolism and rare hepatotoxicity, use lower starting doses and monitor LFTs with chronic use.

pediatric.allergic_weight_based: 0.25 mg/kg/day or 8 mg/m²/day in 2–3 divided doses (≥2 years).
pediatric.allergic_fixed_≥15: 4 mg q8h initially; usual 12–16 mg/day; may require up to 32 mg/day; max 0.5 mg/kg/day.
pediatric.appetite_stimulation: 0.25 mg/kg/day divided BID; max daily dose ≤6 years: 12 mg/day; 7–14 years: 16 mg/day; ≥15 years: 32 mg/day.
pediatric.cyclic_vomiting: 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day in 1–3 divided doses; max 12 mg/day; often given once at bedtime to reduce daytime sedation.
pediatric.functional_abdominal_pain: 0.04–0.6 mg/kg/day divided BID–TID; age-based max 12–16 mg/day.
pediatric.migraine_prophylaxis: 0.2–0.4 mg/kg/day divided BID (up to 1.5 mg/kg/day in divided doses in some series); age-based max 12–16 mg/day.
pediatric.spasticity: ≥12 years: 4 mg HS, increasing by 4 mg q3–4 days; mean ~16 mg/day, max 36 mg/day (limited efficacy data).

sections.simple_explanation: Adults generally start at 4 mg three times daily and titrate up within a usual range of 12–20 mg/day. Children are dosed based on weight and age, usually 2–4 times per day. In all age groups, doses are adjusted based on clinical response and side effects.

sections.heading: Special Populations
sections.text: Cyproheptadine is primarily a pediatric and young-adult tool in modern practice; it is generally avoided in older adults.
sections.pregnancy: Limited human data do not show a clear teratogenic signal, but numbers are small and first-generation antihistamines are generally not preferred due to sedation and anticholinergic effects. If an oral antihistamine is needed in pregnancy, other agents with more favorable profiles are typically selected.
sections.lactation: Unknown if excreted in breast milk. Given class experience (infant sedation, irritability, possible impact on prolactin and milk production) and product labeling, cyproheptadine is contraindicated in breastfeeding patients.
sections.pediatrics: Widely used off-label in children ≥2 years for appetite stimulation, migraine, CVS, and functional abdominal pain. Requires careful attention to dosing, sedation, behavior change (including paradoxical excitation), and weight/BMI tracking.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid in patients ≥65 years (Beers Criteria) due to potent anticholinergic and sedative properties with increased risk of confusion, falls, constipation, and urinary retention.
sections.hepatic: Use cautiously; cyproheptadine is hepatically metabolized and rare cases of hepatitis and hepatic failure have been described. Consider baseline LFTs and periodic monitoring if long-term therapy is anticipated.
sections.renal: Elimination is diminished in renal insufficiency; start at lower doses and titrate slowly, monitoring for enhanced or prolonged effects.
sections.high_risk_occupations: Avoid use in pilots, commercial drivers, and others who require sustained alertness and psychomotor performance.

sections.heading: Monitoring Recommendations
items: Sedation and cognitive effects: Assess daytime somnolence, attention, and psychomotor performance—especially in school-aged children and those in safety-sensitive roles.
Weight/BMI and metabolic profile: At baseline and regularly in appetite-stimulation, migraine, and CVS uses; intervene early if excessive weight gain occurs.
Bowel and urinary function: Ask about constipation, urinary hesitancy, or retention at each visit, particularly if combined with other anticholinergic drugs.
Liver function tests: consider baseline and periodic LFTs in long-term therapy, higher dose regimens, or in people with existing liver disease or on other hepatotoxic drugs.
CBC: Not required routinely, but obtain if clinical signs suggest cytopenias (recurrent infections, bruising, fatigue).
Behavior and sleep in children: Monitor for paradoxical excitation, irritability, insomnia, or behavioral disinhibition.
Medication reconciliation: Regularly review all prescription, OTC, and herbal products to quantify total sedative and anticholinergic burden.

sections.heading: Formulations
sections.text: Cyproheptadine is available in tablet and syrup formulations, which facilitates weight-based pediatric dosing and administration via enteral tubes.
items: Enteral tube administration: Syrup can be diluted with at least an equal volume of purified water; tablets can be crushed and dispersed in water. Hold enteral feeds during administration, flush before and after dosing to maintain tube patency.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Cyproheptadine is a potent first-generation antihistamine (H1 antagonist) with additional antiserotonergic and anticholinergic activity. It competitively blocks histamine at H1 receptors in the GI tract, blood vessels, and respiratory tract, and antagonizes serotonin (notably 5-HT2). The antihistaminic effects explain efficacy in allergic disease, while the antiserotonergic activity underlies its use in serotonin syndrome and possibly migraine/CVS prophylaxis. Its appetite-stimulating effects are thought to be related to antagonism at hypothalamic serotonin receptors that normally suppress feeding. Anticholinergic and H1 blockade mediate sedation and typical first-generation antihistamine adverse effects.

sections.heading: Place in Psychiatric & Pediatric Practice
sections.text:
In contemporary practice, cyproheptadine is seldom used as a primary antihistamine but occupies a niche role in child and adolescent psychiatry, pediatric oncology, and consultation-liaison settings. It is often considered when:

• An underweight child with chronic disease or feeding difficulties needs an appetite stimulant after behavioral and nutritional strategies have been optimized.
• A younger child with migraine or cyclic vomiting requires a low-cost, sedating preventive agent where modest weight gain is acceptable.
• Moderate serotonin syndrome persists despite discontinuation of serotonergic drugs, benzodiazepines, and supportive care.

Given its strong anticholinergic and sedating profile, cyproheptadine is generally avoided in older adults and in any patient with significant delirium risk or high anticholinergic burden. It is best used as a targeted, time-limited intervention with clear treatment goals, objective monitoring of weight and adverse effects, and a plan for reassessment and discontinuation if goals are not met.

faqs.q: When might this medicine be used to boost appetite?
faqs.a: It may be considered for underweight children or teens with a long-term medical or psychiatric condition (e.g., cancer, cystic fibrosis, neurodevelopmental conditions) when nutrition support and behavior strategies are already in place and weight is still not improving. Clear goals are set (e.g., a target weight gain or keeping weight steady), the trial is time-limited (e.g., 8–12 weeks), and weight, BMI and other body measures are checked. It should not be used long-term by default in children at a normal weight or above.

faqs.q: How is it dosed to prevent migraines in children?
faqs.a: A typical dose is 0.2–0.4 mg/kg/day split into two doses (max 12 mg/day for ages 3–6; 16 mg/day for age 7 and up). It starts at the low end and is raised every 1–2 weeks depending on how well it works and how sleepy it makes your child. Giving more of the dose at night can make it easier to tolerate. The benefit is judged over several weeks; if it does not help or causes too many side effects, a different preventive medicine is tried.

faqs.q: How is it used in serotonin syndrome?
faqs.a: It is an add-on treatment for moderate serotonin syndrome when agitation or muscle symptoms continue even after the medicines raising serotonin have been stopped, benzodiazepines given, and supportive care provided. A common plan is a 12 mg loading dose by mouth, then 2 mg every 2 hours until things improve, then 4–8 mg every 6 hours as needed, up to 32 mg/day. It does not replace the basic steps (stopping the medicines, benzodiazepines, supportive care) and is usually not needed in mild cases.

faqs.q: Why is it discouraged in older adults?
faqs.a: It is a sedating antihistamine with strong drying effects. In older adults it greatly raises the risk of sudden confusion (delirium), falls, constipation, being unable to pee, and decline in thinking and memory. The Beers Criteria recommend avoiding it in people 65 and older whatever the reason for use. Medicines without drying effects should be chosen first.

faqs.q: What happens if weight gain on this medicine is too much?
faqs.a: First, your prescriber will look again at why it was started and whether a medicine to boost appetite is still needed. A structured eating plan and physical activity may help. If weight gain goes beyond the goal, or BMI moves into the overweight or obese range, the dose is lowered step by step and stopped, and other approaches are considered. Adding other psychiatric medicines that cause weight gain is avoided where possible.

faqs.q: Do you need regular blood tests on this medicine?
faqs.a: No lab tests are required, but a practical approach includes checking weight and BMI at the start and from time to time; liver blood tests may be considered with long-term or higher-dose use or if you take other medicines that can harm the liver; and a blood count is done if there are signs of low blood cells. Closer checks are reasonable for people at higher risk or with complex medical needs.

faqs.q: Can it be used as a sleep aid?
faqs.a: Although it can make it easier to fall asleep, it is generally a poor choice as a main sleep medicine because of strong drying effects and because the sleepy effect wears off over time. Safer, more targeted options for insomnia should be tried first. If its sleepiness is used as a side benefit (e.g., in a low-weight child with migraine), this should be written into the treatment plan and reviewed from time to time.

faqs.q: How long is it usually taken for appetite before it is reviewed?
faqs.a: For appetite, many clinicians use a time-limited trial (e.g., 8–12 weeks) with goals set in advance (weight gain, better growth, better eating). If the goals are met, the dose may be carefully lowered to see whether the gains last without the medicine. Long, open-ended use should lead to a fresh look at risks and benefits, especially once BMI is normal or above target.

seo.title: Cyproheptadine (Periactin): Dosing, Off-Label Uses, and Safety for Psychiatrists
seo.description: Clinician-focused overview of cyproheptadine: pharmacology, pediatric appetite stimulation, migraine and CVS prophylaxis, serotonin syndrome adjunctive use, dosing strategies, anticholinergic risks, and monitoring.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content oriented to psychiatrists and pediatric prescribers, aligned with current product labeling, Beers Criteria, and contemporary guideline-based use of cyproheptadine as a second-line or adjunctive agent.
